meta.about: Grammar patterns for section 3.3 tier 4, matched over Kuromoji/janome IPADIC tokens. Read by :ml:analysis (GrammarRules.kt) and staged into the APK's assets alongside sfx_dict.json.
meta.attribution: JLPT levels follow the lists at tanos.co.uk, CC BY, Jonathan Waller. Explanations are written for this app.
meta.schema: A match element may constrain surface / base / reading / pos / posNot / cform / ctype. pos and cform are PREFIX matches against the comma-joined IPADIC tag string and the conjugation form. 'after' and 'before' constrain the neighbouring token without consuming it. 'atEnd' requires the match to end on the region's last token. Longest match wins at each position; matches do not overlap; the scan runs left to right. Explanations may interpolate {prev} {prevBase} {base} {text}. Matches and neighbour constraints do not cross sentence-ending punctuation.
meta.caution: These patterns are written against real IPADIC output, not against intuition. IPADIC is full of surprises: によって is ONE token, なきゃ is one token based on ない, たら bases to た, なら bases to だ, and the imperative appears only in the conjugation form (命令ｅ / 命令ｒｏ / 命令ｉ, with full-width latin). Verify any new rule with tools/check_grammar_rules.py before trusting it.

Describes the manner, state or appearance of the noun it attaches to.
Sets what the sentence is about. It is not the subject — it is the frame everything after it is said inside.
Marks who or what is doing the verb. Against は it points at new or contrastive information: は frames, が identifies.
Marks what the verb is done to.
Points at a destination, a time, or the person on the receiving end. Its job depends entirely on the verb it serves.
Where an action happens, or the tool it happens with — as against に, which is where something ends up.
Joins nouns exhaustively, or marks the person an action is done together with.
Marks the person an action is done together with. The same character between two nouns instead lists them.
Links two nouns, with the owner or category first. Japanese stacks these freely where English needs several words.
Adds this to something already said, and replaces は or が rather than stacking on them.
After a noun, a starting point. After a clause, the reason for what follows.
The far end of a range, in space or in time.
Direction of travel. Softer than に, which insists on arrival.
The thing being compared against.
Limits what precedes it, with no suggestion that it is too little.
Like だけ, but it demands a negative verb and carries the sense that this is not enough.
Invites the listener to agree. It assumes shared ground rather than asking a real question.
Pushes information the speaker thinks the listener does not have yet.
Turns the sentence into a question. Casual speech often drops it and just raises the pitch instead.
After a plain-form verb, a blunt prohibition: don't {prevBase}. Sharp, and usually said downward.
Rough masculine emphasis. Pushes the statement at the listener.
Rough emphasis, often to oneself as much as to anyone listening.
Softens the statement. In manga it is heavily gendered as feminine speech, more than it is in real conversation.
Casual, offhand emphasis — closer to English "y'know" than to anything with meaning.
Wondering aloud, with no real expectation of an answer.
A pouting or defensive reason — "because that's how it is". Contraction of もの.
The て-form links clauses without saying how they relate. Sequence, cause and manner all look identical here; context decides.
Concessive link. Mid-sentence it is a real "but".
Closes the sentence as an aside rather than a claim. Trailing けど softens; it is not a real "but" and nothing is being contrasted.
The same concessive job as けど, one register up.
Gives a reason, presented as simple fact. Softer and less argumentative than から.
Piles up reasons, implying the list could go on.
Two actions at once by the same person. The main one is the second.
A literary ながら. Often carries a note of contradiction: doing this while knowing better.
Lists representative actions, not exhaustive ones — these among others.

rules.gloss: is doing / is in the state of
rules.explanation: Either an action in progress or a resulting state that still holds. Which one depends on the verb, not on the form.
Spoken contraction of 〜ている. The い is simply dropped, which is what ordinary speech does with it.
Colloquial squeeze of 〜ていて, linking this clause to the next.
Contraction of 〜ていない. States that something has not come to be, rather than that it simply did not happen.
Completion, usually with regret attached. Something happened and cannot be taken back.
Casual contraction of 〜てしまう. Same regret, lighter tone.
Does something now for the sake of later, and leaves it that way.
Casual contraction of 〜ておく.
Does it to find out what happens. The trying is the point, not the succeeding.
Someone else acts, and the speaker benefits. Japanese tracks who the favour flows toward where English usually does not.
The speaker receives the action, having arranged for it. The favour flows toward the speaker.
The speaker does it for someone else. Said about oneself it can sound condescending, which manga uses on purpose.
A blunt 〜てあげる. Downward to an inferior, or defiantly — "just watch me".
Change moving away from the speaker, in space or forward in time.
Change moving toward the speaker, or up to now from the past.
The standard polite request. Still an instruction, however politely it is dressed.
From {prevBase}. れる／られる can mark passive voice, potential ability or respect. The predicate and surrounding context determine which applies.
From {prevBase}. れる／られる can mark passive voice, potential ability or respect. The predicate and surrounding context determine which applies.
Causative of {prevBase}: makes or lets someone do it. Which of the two depends on who had the choice.
Causative of {prevBase}: makes or lets someone do it.
Plain negative. The casual counterpart of 〜ません.
Plain past. Japanese has one past tense and leans on context for everything English splits into perfect and simple.
The polite verb ending. It says nothing about the content — only about the speaker's stance toward whoever is listening.
Polite negative: ます plus ん.
The polite copula. Attaches to nouns and adjectives to make the sentence polite without changing what it says.
The plain copula. Casual speech drops it entirely as often as it says it.
The speaker's own desire. Japanese avoids using it for other people's wants — you cannot see inside someone else.
Someone else's desire, reported from the outside — which is why it needs its own form.
Hearsay. The speaker got this from somewhere else and is not vouching for it.
A guess from appearance. On the verb stem it means "about to"; on an adjective, "looks".
Casual comparison or guess. The conversational cousin of 〜のよう.
A measured inference, one register above みたい.
A guess offered for agreement. Said flat it is a prediction; said up it is a challenge.
Volitional. Either a suggestion to do it together or the speaker resolving to do it alone.
Bare imperative of {base}. The bluntest way to tell someone to do something — an order, not a request.
A command from above: parent to child, teacher to student. Polite in form, not in power.
The everyday conditional. Once this happens, the rest follows — and it is happy with one-off, concrete situations.
A conditional stated as a general rule rather than a particular occasion.
Takes what was just said as given and responds to it. "If that's how it is, then —".
Automatic consequence. One thing always follows the other, with no choice in it.
Contraction of 〜なければ. The "or else" half is left unsaid, which is what makes it sound urgent.
Contraction of 〜なくては, with the consequence left hanging.
Frames the sentence as explanation rather than news — the reason behind something already on the table.
The written form of 〜んだ. Explains, or insists.
Marks the end of quoted or reported speech. Japanese closes the quote before naming the verb of saying.
Casual quotation, and also a casual topic marker. Which one it is depends on what follows it.
Turns the clause before it into a noun, so it can take a particle like any other.
Connects an agent, means, cause or basis of variation to the predicate. The complete clause determines which relationship applies.
Marks the matter under discussion; につき can also express a basis, reason or a per-unit rate. Context determines which applies.
Honorific for いる, 来る and 行く at once. Raises whoever is being spoken about.
Honorific for 言う.
Honorific for する.
Humble for する. Lowers the speaker, which raises the listener.
Humble for 言う, and the standard way to give one's own name formally.
Humble for もらう. The speaker is on the receiving end and says so deferentially.
Archaic copula. In manga it marks samurai speech, or someone affecting it.
Attributive form of the classical copula なり. Modern Japanese would use の here; the old form gives the phrase a scriptural ring.
Classical negative, where modern Japanese says ない. Formal, literary, or deliberately old-fashioned.
The written copula, used in essays and declarations. Never in ordinary speech.
Corner brackets are Japanese quotation marks. What sits inside them is being named or quoted, not asserted.
{prev} plus する. A large part of the Japanese verb stock is a noun with する attached, and it inflects like any other verb.
Pure contempt for whoever did the action. There is no polite way to translate it.
Casual negative copula. Said falling it denies; said rising it insists on agreement.
Squeezed 〜じゃない, seeking agreement. Casual and regional, and very common in manga dialogue.
